relationships.description: Completing this step of the user journey leads the user directly on to the next step, establishing the order and branching of actions within the same user workflow.
relationships.evidence: The workflow definition in product documentation lists the destination step as the successor (or a conditional branch) of the source step within the same UserWorkflow, e.g. via an ordered sequence or a 'next' field.

relationships.description: The action or experience described by this step is carried out by, and delivers its observable result to, the named user archetype at that point in the journey.
relationships.evidence: The workflow or step specification names the persona as the actor or beneficiary of the step, e.g. a persona field or a 'As <persona>, I…' statement in the journey map.

relationships.description: Accomplishing this step depends on the product possessing the stated ability, such as payment processing or full-text search, regardless of which feature delivers it.
relationships.evidence: The step definition or journey map annotates the step with the capability it relies on, or a capability map traces the capability to the step's observable result.

relationships.description: The user performs this step by directly invoking or perceiving the specific user-facing feature, such as a command, setting or behaviour, that makes the action possible.
relationships.evidence: The product spec or user story for the step references the feature by identifier, or the feature's acceptance criteria cite the step as a usage scenario.

notes: The two 'uses' relationships overlap: features realise capabilities, so step→capability can usually be derived from step→feature→capability. Keep the capability link only for steps whose feature is not yet defined. 'serves' toward a persona is loose, since the persona performs the step; 'performed-by' would read more naturally.
